script.opening: "Hi doctor. It's a bit embarrassing — I'm just so bloated all the time, my tummy feels swollen and I get full after a few mouthfuls. I'm sure it's just my age, or maybe IBS — my friend has that. Could you give me something for the bloating, maybe those peppermint capsules? I almost didn't bother coming, it feels silly making a fuss over a bit of bloating."

facts.text: If asked: about eight weeks, there most days and not going down overnight — "my jeans won't do up any more". Not related to particular foods.
Full after a few mouthfuls, so you are eating less. You think you may have lost a few pounds, though your waist is bigger.
A dull ache low in your tummy and pelvis, on and off, most days. Passing urine more often and more urgently for the last month — no burning, no blood.
Bowels a bit more constipated than usual. No blood from the back passage, no black stools. No vaginal bleeding since your periods stopped at 51.
If asked: you have never had IBS or tummy trouble before this year.
Periods stopped at 51, never on HRT. Two children. No regular medicines, no allergies. Up to date with smears and mammograms.
54, school receptionist, married to Phil. Never smoked, a glass of wine at weekends.
"My auntie — Dad's sister — had ovarian trouble and died in her fifties. Nobody really talked about it." No breast cancer in the family that you know of.
Your auntie has been on your mind; you looked up "bloating" and saw ovarian cancer, then told yourself not to be silly. Say this only if the doctor asks what worries you or about the family.

Apologetic, embarrassed, minimising. If the doctor asks careful questions you answer honestly. If they say you were right to come and explain they want to check carefully — a blood test, a scan and an examination in person — you are relieved to be taken seriously. If they mention cancer bluntly you become frightened; if they explain honestly that tests are to be thorough and most bloating is not cancer, you cope well.

ice.ideas: "It's my age, or maybe IBS like my friend."
ice.concerns: Underneath (only if asked): your auntie's "ovarian trouble".
ice.expectations: "Something for the bloating, like peppermint capsules." You will accept tests if they are explained calmly.

cues: "I get full after a few mouthfuls." — say in the opening.
"It feels silly making a fuss." — say in the opening.
"My auntie had ovarian trouble." — say only if family history is asked.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the OVARIAN-CANCER symptom cluster — PERSISTENT bloating/distension, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary urgency/frequency, especially frequent and in a woman ≥50 — and does NOT accept the "IBS/getting older" framing or prescribe peppermint for it
Knows that NEW IBS-type symptoms presenting for the FIRST time over age 50 warrant investigation (ovarian and bowel cancer consideration), not an IBS label

Carries out the NICE NG12 pathway: arranges a face-to-face abdominal and pelvic examination for a mass or ascites (not possible over video), measures serum CA-125, and arranges an URGENT DIRECT-ACCESS abdominal/pelvic ULTRASOUND if CA-125 is at or above the age-specific threshold (31 IU/mL at 50–59 — not the superseded single 35 IU/mL cut-off) — with a suspected cancer pathway referral straight away if examination finds ascites and/or a pelvic or abdominal mass (not obviously fibroids), or if the ultrasound suggests ovarian cancer; tagged NICE NG12
Weights the risk/associations appropriately (post-menopausal, age, family history of ovarian/breast cancer) and considers the bowel-cancer differential too — without delaying the ovarian work-up

Balances honesty and reassurance: explains the tests are to be thorough and that most such symptoms aren’t cancer, while taking the cluster seriously — avoiding both false reassurance and catastrophising
Surfaces the unspoken fear (the aunt’s "ovarian trouble") gently, validates that she was RIGHT to come (not "making a fuss"), and does not collude with the "it’s silly/just my age" minimisation
Handles embarrassment and the "wasting your time" worry with warmth so she engages with the work-up rather than disengaging

Safety-nets and follows up: the CA-125/ultrasound plan (her threshold is 31 IU/mL) and the suspected cancer pathway criteria, what symptoms warrant sooner review, the timeframe and what to expect, and a follow-up to go through results — ensuring the work-up happens

worked.txt: "First, please don’t apologise — you were absolutely right to come, and this is not silly at all. Persistent bloating, feeling full quickly, and needing the loo more often, going on for two months in a woman your age — that’s exactly the kind of thing I want to see, not brush off. So let’s take it seriously together."

"I know IBS gets blamed for bloating — but here’s an important thing: brand-new tummy symptoms that start for the first time after 50 we don’t just call IBS, because occasionally they’re a sign of something in the ovaries or bowel we’d want to catch early. That’s not me saying it IS that — it’s me saying we check properly rather than assume."

"So here’s what I’d do: ask you to come in today or tomorrow so I can examine your tummy and pelvis properly — I can’t do that over video — and arrange a blood test called CA-125. For your age, if it’s 31 or above, I’ll arrange an urgent ultrasound scan of your tummy and pelvis. There’s clear guidance — NICE NG12 — for exactly these symptoms, and it’s about being thorough. If I felt a lump or any fluid when I examine you, I’d refer you straight to the specialist team on the urgent suspected cancer pathway without waiting for the blood test — but most of the time these tests are reassuring."

"Can I gently ask — you mentioned your aunt had ovarian trouble. Has it crossed your mind that this might be something like that? … Thank you for telling me. That fear makes complete sense, and it’s exactly why getting it checked is the right thing — so you’re not lying awake wondering. Naming it isn’t making a fuss; it’s being sensible."

"Two honest things at once: the great majority of women with these symptoms do NOT have anything sinister, and the tests are mostly to put your mind at rest. And, because the symptoms fit a pattern we take seriously, we do them promptly rather than wait and see. Both true."

"I’ll examine you in person, sort the CA-125 and the scan if needed, and we’ll go through the results together. If meanwhile the bloating gets worse, you can’t eat, you lose weight, or get any bleeding, tell me sooner. You came in worried you were wasting my time — the opposite is true; you’ve done exactly the right thing."

f.learning: Persistent (not fluctuating) bloating/distension, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain and urinary urgency/frequency — especially frequent and in a woman ≥50 — is the classic symptom cluster of OVARIAN CANCER, which notoriously hides as "IBS" or "getting older". A key NICE NG12 caution: NEW IBS-type symptoms presenting for the first time over age 50 should be investigated (ovarian AND bowel cancer), not labelled IBS. The pathway is to examine for a mass/ascites, measure serum CA-125, arrange an urgent direct-access abdominal/pelvic ultrasound if CA-125 is at or above the age-specific threshold (31 IU/mL at 50–59 since April 2026; the old single 35 IU/mL cut-off is superseded), and refer on a suspected cancer pathway straight away if examination finds ascites and/or a pelvic or abdominal mass (not obviously fibroids) or the ultrasound suggests ovarian cancer — after a video call the examination needs a face-to-face appointment — the very presentation NG12 exists to catch, so prescribing peppermint for it is the dangerous error. The examinable hidden agenda is minimisation ("it’s silly, just my age") masking a real, unspoken fear (an aunt’s "ovarian trouble"); surface and validate it, affirm she was right to come rather than "making a fuss", balance honesty with reassurance (most such symptoms aren’t cancer; we test to be thorough), and ensure the work-up happens.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG61 (2008, updated 2017) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
knowledge.summary: Eight weeks of persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic discomfort and urinary frequency in a 54-year-old is the ovarian-cancer symptom pattern, and new IBS-type symptoms over 50 are investigated, not labelled. Examine, check CA-125 against her age threshold, and scan if raised.

points.t: NICE NG12: in women aged 40 and over with persistent or frequent symptoms — particularly more than 12 times a month — of abdominal distension or bloating, early satiety or loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, or increased urinary urgency or frequency, measure serum CA-125 in primary care.

NICE NG12: carry out appropriate tests for ovarian cancer in any woman aged 50 or over who has had symptoms within the last 12 months suggestive of IBS, because IBS rarely presents for the first time at this age. NICE CG61 also lists new symptoms after 50 among the features that need further assessment.

NICE NG12 replaced the single 35 IU/mL cut-off with age bands for urgent direct-access ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis: 35 IU/mL at 40–49, 31 IU/mL at 50–59, 24 IU/mL at 60–69, 25 IU/mL at 70–79 and 31 IU/mL at 80 and over. For Sandra, at 54, the threshold is 31 IU/mL.

points.h: Examination can bypass the blood test
points.t: NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway if examination finds ascites and/or a pelvic or abdominal mass that is not obviously uterine fibroids. A video call cannot do this — arrange a face-to-face abdominal and pelvic examination promptly.

Ultrasound suggesting ovarian cancer → suspected cancer pathway referral. If CA-125 is below threshold, or the scan is normal, assess for other causes (including bowel) and ask her to return if symptoms persist or become more frequent — a normal CA-125 does not close the question on its own.

Age, post-menopausal status and a family history of ovarian or breast cancer raise concern but do not decide the work-up. Clarify the aunt’s diagnosis and any other family cancers; significant family history may warrant genetics referral via local pathways.

model.text: Hello Mrs Whitlock, I’m Dr Patel. Thanks for booking — how can I help today?
model.why: Open start, lets her set out the problem

model.text: It’s a bit embarrassing. I’m bloated all the time, my tummy feels swollen, and I’m full after a few mouthfuls. It’s probably my age, or IBS — my friend has that. Could I have something for it, maybe peppermint capsules? I nearly didn’t bother coming.
Please don’t apologise — I’m really glad you came. I’d like to ask some questions, explain what I think, and agree what to do together. Is that alright?
model.why: Counters the “wasting time” worry at once and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, of course.
How long has the bloating been there, and does it come and go, or is it there most days?
model.why: Establishes persistence and frequency — the NICE NG12 criteria

model.text: About eight weeks. It’s pretty much there all the time now, not like a bit of wind that goes.
Any pain in your tummy or pelvis? And has anything changed with your waterworks?
A sort of low ache down below. And I’m going to the loo more often — I thought that was age too.
Have you had tummy trouble like this before, or is this new for you?
model.why: New IBS-type symptoms over 50 are a flag

model.text: No, it’s new. I’ve never had a dodgy stomach.
Any bleeding from the back passage? Any change in your weight or appetite?
model.why: Screens bowel red flags and weight loss

model.text: No bleeding from the back passage. My appetite’s less because I fill up so fast.
Does anyone in your family have a history of bowel, ovarian or breast problems?
model.why: Family history, which opens the door to her fear

model.text: My aunt had… ovarian trouble. I don’t really know the details. It wasn’t talked about.
I noticed you paused there. Has it crossed your mind that this might be something like what your aunt had?
model.why: Picks up the cue and names the unspoken fear gently

model.text: …Yes. I’ve been lying awake about it. I didn’t want to say it out loud in case you thought I was being silly.
Thank you for telling me. That isn’t silly — it’s a sensible worry, and it’s exactly why I want to check properly rather than guess.
model.why: Validates the fear and her decision to come

model.text: Let me be honest with you. Bloating that’s there most days, feeling full quickly, a pelvic ache and needing the loo more — especially when it starts for the first time after 50 — is a pattern we always check for the ovaries, rather than calling it IBS.
model.why: Refuses the IBS/age framing and explains why

model.text: So you do think it could be cancer?
Most women with these symptoms don’t have cancer. But the pattern fits one we take seriously, so we test promptly rather than wait and see. Both things are true.
model.why: Balances honesty with reassurance, no catastrophising

model.text: Okay. I’d rather know.

Here’s the plan. I need to examine your tummy and pelvis in person — could you come in today or tomorrow? You’re welcome to have a chaperone. I’ll also arrange a blood test called CA-125, a urine test, and some routine bloods.
model.why: Face-to-face examination for mass/ascites plus CA-125

model.text: I can come tomorrow morning.

Good. For your age, if the CA-125 is 31 or above, I’ll arrange an urgent ultrasound of your tummy and pelvis. If I feel a lump or any fluid when I examine you, I’d refer you straight to the specialist team on the urgent suspected cancer pathway — without waiting for the blood test.
model.why: NICE NG12 age-specific threshold and the direct-referral route

model.text: And if it’s all normal?

Then I’d look at other causes, including the bowel, and I’d still want to see you if the symptoms carry on — one normal test doesn’t mean we stop listening. I won’t give you peppermint instead of the tests, but it’s fine alongside if it helps.
model.why: Plans for a normal result without false reassurance

model.text: If your tummy swells quickly, you can’t keep food down, you notice weight loss or any bleeding, or you get severe pain, contact us the same day. I’ll ring you with the CA-125 result myself, so you’re not left waiting.
model.why: Specific safety-net and ownership of the result

model.text: Thank you. I feel better for saying it out loud.
You did exactly the right thing. So — examination tomorrow, CA-125 and bloods, a scan if needed, and I’ll call you. What will you tell your family about today?
That I’m having it checked properly, and it’s not just my age.

social.t: Many women delay with bloating because it feels trivial or embarrassing. Explicitly affirming that she was right to come makes her more likely to return if symptoms persist.
An aunt’s illness that “wasn’t talked about” shapes fear and silence. Invite her to find out more from relatives if she feels able to.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones: explain why the examination is needed, get consent, offer a chaperone and record the discussion. A video consultation cannot replace it.

professional.t: Where examination could change management, arrange it face to face promptly (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: good clinical care). Document the plan and the reason.
Safety-netting includes a system to ensure the CA-125 and any scan are acted on — a named person to check the result, and tracking of any suspected cancer referral.

community.t: Target Ovarian Cancer and Ovarian Cancer Action for symptom information; Macmillan if a cancer is diagnosed; local genetics service if family history is significant.

redFlags: Persistent or frequent bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary urgency or frequency at 40+ — NICE NG12
New IBS-type symptoms at 50+ — test for ovarian cancer rather than label
Palpable mass or ascites — suspected cancer pathway referral
psychosocial: Embarrassment and fear of “wasting the doctor’s time”
Family silence about the aunt’s illness
ice: Idea: “It’s my age, or IBS like my friend”
Concern: the unspoken fear that it is what her aunt had
Expectation: peppermint capsules and to be sent away

playbook.diagnosis: Honest and balanced: “This pattern, starting after 50, is one we always check for the ovaries. Most women with it don’t have cancer — but we test promptly rather than wait.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of it like a smoke alarm going off — usually it’s burnt toast, but you always check the kitchen. The blood test and, if needed, a scan are how we check.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried this might be like your aunt’s illness. That’s a sensible worry, and it’s exactly why I want to check properly.”
management.psychosocial: Make it easy to attend: examination at a time she can manage, a chaperone offered, and a named person ringing her with the result.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face abdominal and pelvic examination promptly; suspected cancer pathway referral if mass or ascites
CA-125 — at 54, 31 IU/mL or above → urgent direct-access abdominal and pelvic ultrasound (NICE NG12)
If tests are normal: consider other causes including bowel; review if symptoms persist
safetyNet: Rapid swelling, unable to eat, weight loss, bleeding or severe pain → same-day contact
Result call booked; return if symptoms persist or become more frequent despite normal tests

pitfalls.intro: This station is designed to catch the doctor who agrees with the patient. The clinical marks come from refusing the IBS label and knowing the current NICE NG12 pathway; the relating marks come from finding the fear she won’t say.

items.fail: Prescribing peppermint or an antispasmodic for “IBS” with no tests.
items.why: New IBS-type symptoms at 50+ and the persistent ovarian cluster both require tests under NICE NG12.
items.fix: “New tummy symptoms after 50 we check properly rather than calling them IBS.” Then arrange examination and CA-125.

items.fail: Quoting a single CA-125 cut-off of 35 IU/mL.
items.why: Since April 2026, NICE NG12 uses age-specific thresholds; at 54 it is 31 IU/mL. An outdated threshold could miss a raised result.
items.fix: Know the band for the patient in front of you, or say “above the threshold for your age”.

items.fail: Arranging bloods over video and never examining her.
items.why: A mass or ascites on examination triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral straight away, without waiting for CA-125.
items.fix: “I need to examine you in person — can you come in today or tomorrow?”

items.fail: Hearing “my aunt had ovarian trouble” and moving on to the next question.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The fear is her real reason for attending.
items.fix: “Has it crossed your mind this might be something like that?” Then validate before explaining.

items.fail: Swinging from reassurance to alarm — “it’s probably nothing” followed by “we need to rule out cancer urgently”.
items.why: Inconsistent messages increase anxiety and reduce trust.
items.fix: Say both truths together: most women with these symptoms don’t have cancer, and the pattern means we test promptly.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll let you know if anything’s abnormal”.
items.why: Leaves no plan for persistent symptoms with a normal CA-125, and no named safety-net.
items.fix: Own the result, name same-day symptoms, and say what happens if tests are normal but symptoms continue.

timeMap.d: She apologises for coming. Tell her she was right to — it unlocks the rest.
Duration, persistence and frequency; early satiety, pelvic pain, urinary symptoms; new versus lifelong; bleeding and weight.
The aunt’s “ovarian trouble” is the cue. Name the fear gently and validate it.
Why this isn’t labelled IBS. Examination in person; CA-125 against her age threshold; ultrasound if raised; suspected cancer referral if mass or ascites.
Named symptoms, who will give her the result, and teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “age or IBS”, prescribes peppermint, and closes; never asks about persistence, urinary symptoms or family history; misses the fear behind the pause; or quotes an outdated CA-125 threshold and no examination.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the ovarian symptom pattern and that new IBS-type symptoms over 50 need tests; arranges examination and CA-125, with ultrasound if raised; acknowledges her worry; gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: surfaces the unspoken fear about her aunt and validates it; states the age-specific threshold correctly; explains the direct route if a mass or ascites is found; balances honesty and reassurance in plain words; owns the result and plans for persistent symptoms despite a normal test.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably IBS — try peppermint capsules and see how you go.”
avoid.instead: “New tummy symptoms after 50 are something we always check properly, rather than calling them IBS.”
avoid.why: This is the exact presentation NICE NG12 is designed to catch.

avoid.dont: “I’m sure it’s nothing to worry about.”
avoid.instead: “Most women with these symptoms don’t have cancer — and because the pattern matters, we’ll test promptly.”
avoid.why: False reassurance before tests undermines trust if the result is abnormal.

avoid.dont: “Your CA-125 was normal, so you’re fine.”
avoid.instead: “That result is reassuring, but if the symptoms carry on I still want to see you.”
avoid.why: CA-125 can be normal in some ovarian cancers; persistent symptoms need reassessment.

You did exactly the right thing. So — examination tomorrow, CA-125 and bloods, a scan if needed, and I’ll call you. What will you tell your family about today?
That I’m having it checked properly, and it’s not just my age.

SCA_STEM.name: Sandra Whitlock
pmh: No previous diagnosis of IBS on record
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent consultations or blood tests. Family history: aunt had “ovarian trouble” (details unknown).

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG61 (2008, updated 2017) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Eight weeks of persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic discomfort and urinary frequency in a 54-year-old is the ovarian-cancer symptom pattern, and new IBS-type symptoms over 50 are investigated, not labelled. Examine, check CA-125 against her age threshold, and scan if raised.

points.t: NICE NG12: in women aged 40 and over with persistent or frequent symptoms — particularly more than 12 times a month — of abdominal distension or bloating, early satiety or loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, or increased urinary urgency or frequency, measure serum CA-125 in primary care.

NICE NG12: carry out appropriate tests for ovarian cancer in any woman aged 50 or over who has had symptoms within the last 12 months suggestive of IBS, because IBS rarely presents for the first time at this age. NICE CG61 also lists new symptoms after 50 among the features that need further assessment.

NICE NG12 replaced the single 35 IU/mL cut-off with age bands for urgent direct-access ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis: 35 IU/mL at 40–49, 31 IU/mL at 50–59, 24 IU/mL at 60–69, 25 IU/mL at 70–79 and 31 IU/mL at 80 and over. For Sandra, at 54, the threshold is 31 IU/mL.

points.h: Examination can bypass the blood test
points.t: NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway if examination finds ascites and/or a pelvic or abdominal mass that is not obviously uterine fibroids. A video call cannot do this — arrange a face-to-face abdominal and pelvic examination promptly.

Ultrasound suggesting ovarian cancer → suspected cancer pathway referral. If CA-125 is below threshold, or the scan is normal, assess for other causes (including bowel) and ask her to return if symptoms persist or become more frequent — a normal CA-125 does not close the question on its own.

Age, post-menopausal status and a family history of ovarian or breast cancer raise concern but do not decide the work-up. Clarify the aunt’s diagnosis and any other family cancers; significant family history may warrant genetics referral via local pathways.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; lets her describe the bloating and her own explanation before responding to the peppermint request.
Embarrassment, reluctance to “make a fuss”, and how the symptoms are affecting eating and sleep.
Picked up the pause about the aunt’s “ovarian trouble” and the minimising “just my age”.
Idea (age or IBS), the unspoken fear of what her aunt had, and her wish for peppermint and to be sent away.
Face-to-face abdominal and pelvic examination with chaperone offered; CA-125; urinalysis; FBC and routine bloods.
Ovarian cancer versus bowel pathology versus benign causes; recognises new IBS-type symptoms at 50+ are not IBS until proven.
Established persistence and frequency; asked about bleeding, weight and appetite; knows mass or ascites triggers direct referral.
Persistent symptoms needing investigation for ovarian cancer — shared honestly, with the balance that most are not cancer.
NICE NG12: CA-125 with her age threshold (31 IU/mL at 50–59) → urgent direct-access ultrasound; suspected cancer pathway if mass, ascites or suggestive scan.
Clarifies family history of ovarian or breast cancer and considers genetics referral if significant; plans for other causes if tests are normal.
Owns the result; named symptoms for same-day contact; review if symptoms persist despite normal tests.

social.t: Many women delay with bloating because it feels trivial or embarrassing. Explicitly affirming that she was right to come makes her more likely to return if symptoms persist.
An aunt’s illness that “wasn’t talked about” shapes fear and silence. Invite her to find out more from relatives if she feels able to.

legal.t: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones: explain why the examination is needed, get consent, offer a chaperone and record the discussion. A video consultation cannot replace it.

professional.t: Where examination could change management, arrange it face to face promptly (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: good clinical care). Document the plan and the reason.
Safety-netting includes a system to ensure the CA-125 and any scan are acted on — a named person to check the result, and tracking of any suspected cancer referral.

community.t: Target Ovarian Cancer and Ovarian Cancer Action for symptom information; Macmillan if a cancer is diagnosed; local genetics service if family history is significant.

redFlags: Persistent or frequent bloating, early satiety, pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary urgency or frequency at 40+ — NICE NG12
New IBS-type symptoms at 50+ — test for ovarian cancer rather than label
Palpable mass or ascites — suspected cancer pathway referral
psychosocial: Embarrassment and fear of “wasting the doctor’s time”
Family silence about the aunt’s illness
ice: Idea: “It’s my age, or IBS like my friend”
Concern: the unspoken fear that it is what her aunt had
Expectation: peppermint capsules and to be sent away

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Honest and balanced: “This pattern, starting after 50, is one we always check for the ovaries. Most women with it don’t have cancer — but we test promptly rather than wait.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of it like a smoke alarm going off — usually it’s burnt toast, but you always check the kitchen. The blood test and, if needed, a scan are how we check.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried this might be like your aunt’s illness. That’s a sensible worry, and it’s exactly why I want to check properly.”
management.psychosocial: Make it easy to attend: examination at a time she can manage, a chaperone offered, and a named person ringing her with the result.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face abdominal and pelvic examination promptly; suspected cancer pathway referral if mass or ascites
CA-125 — at 54, 31 IU/mL or above → urgent direct-access abdominal and pelvic ultrasound (NICE NG12)
If tests are normal: consider other causes including bowel; review if symptoms persist
safetyNet: Rapid swelling, unable to eat, weight loss, bleeding or severe pain → same-day contact
Result call booked; return if symptoms persist or become more frequent despite normal tests

SCA_LINKS.s: When not to label IBS · CA-125 at 50+

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is designed to catch the doctor who agrees with the patient. The clinical marks come from refusing the IBS label and knowing the current NICE NG12 pathway; the relating marks come from finding the fear she won’t say.

items.fail: Prescribing peppermint or an antispasmodic for “IBS” with no tests.
items.why: New IBS-type symptoms at 50+ and the persistent ovarian cluster both require tests under NICE NG12.
items.fix: “New tummy symptoms after 50 we check properly rather than calling them IBS.” Then arrange examination and CA-125.

items.fail: Quoting a single CA-125 cut-off of 35 IU/mL.
items.why: Since April 2026, NICE NG12 uses age-specific thresholds; at 54 it is 31 IU/mL. An outdated threshold could miss a raised result.
items.fix: Know the band for the patient in front of you, or say “above the threshold for your age”.

items.fail: Arranging bloods over video and never examining her.
items.why: A mass or ascites on examination triggers a suspected cancer pathway referral straight away, without waiting for CA-125.
items.fix: “I need to examine you in person — can you come in today or tomorrow?”

items.fail: Hearing “my aunt had ovarian trouble” and moving on to the next question.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The fear is her real reason for attending.
items.fix: “Has it crossed your mind this might be something like that?” Then validate before explaining.

items.fail: Swinging from reassurance to alarm — “it’s probably nothing” followed by “we need to rule out cancer urgently”.
items.why: Inconsistent messages increase anxiety and reduce trust.
items.fix: Say both truths together: most women with these symptoms don’t have cancer, and the pattern means we test promptly.

items.fail: Closing with “we’ll let you know if anything’s abnormal”.
items.why: Leaves no plan for persistent symptoms with a normal CA-125, and no named safety-net.
items.fix: Own the result, name same-day symptoms, and say what happens if tests are normal but symptoms continue.
